title: Dalton v. Educational Testing Service
summary: ETS had to consider the relevant information it promised to consider, but the remedy was a good-faith reconsideration of the score rather than automatic certification of its validity.
notes: 87 N.Y.2d 384, 663 N.E.2d 289 (1995). The dissenters were Judge Levine, joined by Judge Simons, who pointed to concrete evidence that ETS had considered Dalton's submissions; the trial court had found ETS failed to make even rudimentary efforts to evaluate or investigate the information.

sections.Parties: Brian Dalton, acting through his father, challenged Educational Testing Service’s proposed cancellation of his November SAT score. ETS administered the examination under the conditions in its registration bulletin.
sections.Material Facts:
Dalton’s combined score rose 410 points between May and November 1991. ETS investigated increases above 350 points. Different-looking handwriting on the answer sheets led its examiners to suspect that different people had taken the two tests. The registration agreement allowed cancellation when ETS had reason to question a score’s validity. It also gave the student five options: submit additional information, take a free retest, accept cancellation and a refund, seek review by a receiving institution, or arbitrate.

Dalton chose to submit information. He supplied evidence of mononucleosis during the first test, preparatory-course results consistent with his later score, statements from a proctor and two students placing him at the November examination, and his own handwriting expert’s report. ETS obtained another expert opinion supporting its original concern. The trial court found that the board had treated handwriting as the sole relevant matter and had not meaningfully considered the other evidence.
sections.Procedural History: After a twelve-day nonjury trial, the trial court found a breach of good faith and ordered ETS to release the score. The Appellate Division affirmed. The New York Court of Appeals agreed that ETS breached the agreement but modified the relief to require good-faith consideration of Dalton’s materials.
sections.Issue: What did good faith require when the contract gave ETS discretion to question a score while promising the student a process for responding, and what performance could the court compel?
sections.Holding: ETS breached its promise by failing to consider relevant submitted material. Dalton was entitled to the promised review, not a judicial declaration that his score was valid.
sections.Reasoning:
Contractual discretion means that the agreement leaves a choice or judgment to a party. Good faith constrains how that power is used. Here, evidence of Dalton’s presence and ability directly addressed the suspected impersonation; treating it as irrelevant defeated the review opportunity ETS had offered. Refusing to exercise the promised discretion was itself a contractual failure.

The limit on ETS did not authorize a court to replace it as the examiner. The agreement required a reason to question validity, not proof of cheating. It placed responsibility for submitting information on the student and did not require ETS to conduct an external investigation. After genuinely considering relevant information, ETS retained authority to weigh it and determine validity, subject to the prohibition on arbitrary or irrational action. Specific performance therefore required the review that should have occurred. Compelling release of a fully validated score would award something ETS had never promised. The remaining contractual review options also remained available.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Dalton is the clearest worked example of contractual discretion in this course: identify who has the choice, what process was promised, what facts bear on that choice, and how a remedy can enforce the process without dictating the result.

topics.discretion: ETS could decide score validity, but had to exercise that judgment through its promised consideration of relevant evidence.
topics.good-faith: The implied covenant protects the benefit of the review process without contradicting the express cancellation power.
topics.specific-relief: The court ordered the promised reconsideration rather than a result the contract did not guarantee.
topics.assent: The registration bulletin supplied the express terms against which the implied obligation was measured.
topics.satisfaction: ETS's discretion to cancel a score it had reason to question is a satisfaction-type discretion that good faith constrains.
topics.specific-performance: The remedy debate was whether to order release of the score or only a good-faith reconsideration, a question of specific relief.

learning.separateOpinions: The editors report a dissent by two judges who believed ETS had considered and rejected Dalton’s evidence within its discretion. The dispute concerned what review occurred, not merely a disagreement over the legal existence of good faith.
